headline.main: A Family Taken Hostage by Hamas: "The First Time in 484 Days that I Woke Up without Fear"
headline.social: Life after Hamas Captivity: "The First Time in 484 Days that I Woke Up without Fear"

intro: Two of her children were held captive by Hamas, as was – until a few days ago – their father. Here, Israeli Hadas Kalderon talks about her fight for the release of her family and the difficult return to a normal life.
text:
She has hardly slept, says Hadas Kalderon, 57, as she walks into the lobby of a hotel near Tel Aviv on a Sunday morning in early February. Still, she seems cheerful and upbeat. Fewer than 24 hours earlier, her ex-husband Ofer Kalderon, with whom she has four children, was released by Hamas and admitted to hospital for observation. On October 7, 2023, the now 54-year-old was abducted by terrorists from the Nir Oz kibbutz and taken to the Gaza Strip with his son Erez and daughter Sahar, then 12 and 16 years old respectively. The children were released in late November 2023 as part of the first hostage deal.
Hadas Kalderon survived the massacre in the safe room of her home in Nir Oz together with her son Rotem, now 20. Her mother and 12-year-old niece were murdered. Nir Oz is located just two kilometers from the Gaza Strip and about one in four of the 400 residents was killed or abducted that day by Hamas and other terrorist groups. Hadas Kalderon became one of the leaders of the protest movement to free the hostages.
DER SPIEGEL: Ms. Kalderon, your ex-husband Ofer was just released by Hamas after almost 16 months. Are you relieved?
Kalderon: It's as if a 100-ton weight has been lifted from me. Today is the first time in 484 days that I woke up without fear and worry. I was very afraid that my children would have to grow up without their father. That's why I did everything I could to get him back. Even though we are divorced, I fought for him as if he were still my husband.
DER SPIEGEL: What was it like to see him again for the first time?
Kalderon: I let my children and his relatives go first and only saw him briefly. When I hugged him, he seemed very fragile to me. I sensed that he is not doing well, even if it may appear so on the outside. I could see the pain in his eyes. He now has a long road ahead of him.
DER SPIEGEL: Do you know what he experienced while in captivity?
Kalderon: During the first period of his captivity, Ofer had to spend time in complete darkness and tied up. He was beaten, and was given only half a pita bread a day, so he was very hungry. When my daughter Sahar was later taken there, he had already lost 20 pounds. After the children and women were released, there was even less food than before. For months, Ofer was unable to shower. He was underground the whole time. My children told me what it's like to barely be able to breathe, not knowing whether it's day or night. The air was so humid that they could wring out their mattresses.
DER SPIEGEL: What did your children say about seeing their father again?
Kalderon: That he made them laugh with his jokes. We were asked not to tell him everything that has happened since he was abducted. That my mother and my niece were murdered, that many of his friends have been killed, that his house was destroyed and that the kibbutz basically no longer exists. We answer questions, but we don't tell him anything on our own initiative.
DER SPIEGEL: How do you deal with someone who was held hostage for so long?
Kalderon: When you're held captive, you lose control. That's why it's important to let the released hostages make all the decisions themselves, even the smallest ones.
DER SPIEGEL: He asked for a beer.
Kalderon: Yes, but the medical team advised against it because his body can't handle anything like that yet. He first has to slowly get used to normal food again.
DER SPIEGEL: Did you bring anything for Ofer for the reunion?
Kalderon: His family bought him clothes, socks, towels. His brother even went to his burned-out house to see what shampoo he uses so that he could buy it for him.
DER SPIEGEL: How did you prepare your children to see their father again?
Kalderon: I told them that they have to be prepared for the fact that their father is no longer the same. He was a doer, someone who liked to travel, who found everything easy. But a year and a half underground – that's hard for anyone to bear. We didn't know in what state we would get him back. I think we still don’t know.
DER SPIEGEL: The reunion was filmed. Ofer can be seen embracing his four children; they are laughing and crying at the same time.
Kalderon: Only my youngest son Erez doesn't cry, unlike his siblings. He hasn’t ever cried since he was released by Hamas in November 2023. He is too restrained. That worries me.
DER SPIEGEL: What did your son experience in captivity?
Kalderon: For the first 16 days, he was held alone, without other hostages, in a teacher's apartment. Only after that was he brought to a place where he met others. Erez has told me everything, but he refuses therapy. I try to do things with him that help him, like riding and surfing. I have no illusions, he will never be the same again. He's afraid to shower alone, to sleep alone. I always have to be with him. Even more than a year after their release, my children still fear that they could be kidnapped at any time. Hearing Arabic or seeing pita bread sends them into a panic. They can't be alone with strangers – in a taxi or on a bus, for example.
DER SPIEGEL: Do they go to school?
Kalderon: Rarely. They can't learn and can't concentrate. Their bodies are here, but their souls are still in Gaza. I want to give them everything, but at the same time I have to set limits. It's hard to find the right balance. Sometimes I force them to get up. They sleep poorly. Often they are awake until two or three in the morning, so it's hard for them to get out of bed in the morning.
DER SPIEGEL: How is your daughter Sahar, now 17, coping with what she experienced?
Kalderon: She was last imprisoned with her father. When she was released, she had to leave him behind in that tunnel. When they said goodbye, Ofer cried and said: "Continue living your life, but don't forget me. Please fight for me. I don't want to die here.” That's the story she told me. She was constantly feeling guilty. If Ofer hadn't come back, I don't know what would have become of her.
DER SPIEGEL: Is that another reason why you fought so hard for your ex-husband's release?
Kalderon: Yes, and I told my children that they had to help me. Sometimes I felt bad about it. I knew it wasn't easy for them. They no longer had a home and had lost friends and relatives. They just wanted their normal lives back. And I asked them to fight for their father. They hate being interviewed or photographed. They also refuse to come to the hostage protests.
DER SPIEGEL: Since October 7, you have been one of the loudest voices in the protests of family members, which were increasingly directed against the government. Was that the right approach?
Kalderon: I wasn't concerned with politics; I spoke as a mother. Not with my head, but with my gut, or more precisely, with my uterus. I screamed and cried, I was hysterical, but I didn't care what others thought. I didn't want to be quiet, although the government sent us messages asking us to be quiet. There was also the subliminal threat: if you don't be quiet, the hostages will never come back.
DER SPIEGEL: It is striking that the mothers and sisters of the hostages are playing the leading role in the protests. Why is that?
Kalderon: We women took the protest into our own hands while many men collapsed. At the same time, only men made the decisions in the government and the army – and their thinking followed a military logic from the very beginning. They believed that military pressure would accelerate success in the negotiations.
DER SPIEGEL: Did you feel abandoned by your government?
Kalderon: At the beginning, we believed that our government was on our side. But gradually we realized that they didn't care about us and that our hostages weren't a priority for them. We realized that we had two opponents: Hamas and our government. I'm convinced that our hostages would still be in the hands of the terrorists if it hadn't been for the protest movement. It's possible that many more of them would have been killed.
DER SPIEGEL: What gave you hope during all this time?
Kalderon: After October 7, I was certain that I had lost my children. People thought that I was strong, a fighter, that I had hope. But I had no hope! I had nothing to lose, and that's why I was able to do everything – to go beyond all my limits.
DER SPIEGEL: You have been in a constant state of crisis since October 7. You barely survived and your mother was killed; you first had to fight for your children, then for their father. Are you finally able to think of yourself now?
Kalderon: Maybe that's why I threw myself into this fight to the degree that I did: to distract myself from the pain. I even missed my mother's funeral to meet with French President Emmanuel Macron. The living were more important than the dead. This activism was my salvation. I haven't spoken to a psychologist this entire time. But I kept telling my story, and that has helped me process what I have experienced. My book was also part of this process.
DER SPIEGEL: You grew up in the kibbutz Nir Oz. Will your family go back there one day?
Kalderon: My children want to go back to the kibbutz, but I can't do it. I'm sorry. I'm not going back, no way. Do you know why? Because I'm convinced there will be another October 7.
DER SPIEGEL: What makes you so sure?
Kalderon: The terrorists told my children: "We will be back.” And I believe them. For Hamas, October 7 was a great success. They feel like victors.
DER SPIEGEL: You don’t think the army would be able to prevent a new attack?
Kalderon: We still don't know how October 7 could have happened. We need a commission of inquiry to address the mistakes, only then can we prevent something like this from happening again in the future. I spent more than 10 hours in my safe room that day listening to gunfire, explosions and screams. I felt like I was at the mercy of the terrorists. It was a pogrom, but in our own country, which was supposed to protect us.
DER SPIEGEL: What is your view of the Israeli military operation in Gaza following October 7?
Kalderon: I thought our approach was wrong from the start. It is very painful for me to see the destruction in Gaza. I don't want anyone to get hurt, neither on their side nor on ours. But we must not forget what caused it: Hamas chose to attack us instead of making sure that their people had good lives. They spent millions and millions of dollars on terrorist purposes.
DER SPIEGEL: Many residents of Nir Oz were in favor of coexistence with the Palestinians.
Kalderon: Yes, that's really absurd. Especially many of the older people who were murdered had spent their entire lives working on behalf of the Palestinians. My father was one of them. They brought people from Gaza to hospitals in Israel.
DER SPIEGEL: Do you still believe in peaceful coexistence?
Kalderon: I do believe in it. But Hamas doesn't want peace. That's why we can't allow them to continue ruling over Gaza and spreading their ideology like poison in the schools. If that changes, we might be able to make peace.
DER SPIEGEL: Is your fight finally over?
Kalderon: Our fight won't be over until all the hostages have returned from this hell. For as long as that takes, our lives are frozen in time on October 7. But maybe tomorrow I'll start thinking about the future.
